pos_profile.title: POS 2 — The Point of Sale Profile
pos_profile.desc: The Point of Sale Profile in full: the ten groundwork records and the back-office test sale, items/prices/tax with the one-template rule, the Setup tab, Discount Mode and the override machinery, Payments & Returns with lay-by and staff purchase wiring, the Gift Vouchers tab and its offline policy, Integrations, the user table's access boxes, and the Power Approver table — with Okelewo's three profiles built as the worked example.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The profile: how to approach it
lessons.html:
This module walks through the Point of Sale Profile field by field. It is the longest module in the track because the profile is where every counter rule lives. Before the fields, three working principles.

1. Every setting is a decision. Most fields on the profile have defaults, and a counter will run on the defaults. But a default is still a policy — it just is not one anyone chose. When you set up a profile, go through each consequential field and decide it on purpose. The rest of this module tells you what each field does and what depends on it, so those decisions are informed ones.

2. The right people decide, the administrator enters. The administrator holds the pen, but many settings are really business decisions that belong to specific people. The discount mode is a decision about margin — whoever owns pricing should decide it. The cash refund switch is a decision about money leaving the drawer — whoever owns the money should decide it. The voucher settings belong with whoever runs the voucher programme. A good habit during setup: for each important field, note what was chosen, who chose it, and why. Later, when someone asks why the counter behaves a certain way, the answer is on record instead of in somebody's memory.

3. Changing a live profile is changing the rules. A profile edit takes effect for every sale after it. Extending the return window for one insistent customer, lifting the override requirement for a busy season, enabling negative stock temporarily — each of these changes the counter's rules for everyone, and each is easy to make and easy to forget. Treat profile changes the way you treat the original setup: decided by the right person, noted with a reason, and reviewed periodically. A yearly walk through each profile, comparing the settings against the notes, catches the changes nobody remembers making.

How many profiles? Module 1 gave the rule; here it is again because this module starts by applying it. Use one shared profile where every till in a shop should behave identically — one set of rules, one record to maintain, with terminals still reported individually. Create a separate profile only where a counter genuinely needs different rules — a returns desk with different permissions, a till with different hardware behaviour or a different float. The number of profiles should equal the number of genuinely different policies.

The module's route. Chapter 2 covers the records that must exist before the profile can be created. Chapter 3 covers items, prices, tax and payment methods — the records every scan touches. Chapters 4 to 8 walk the profile itself: the Setup tab, the Pricing & Discounts tab, the Payments & Returns tab, the Gift Vouchers tab, and finally the Integrations tab together with the user table and the Power Approver table. Chapter 9 builds Okelewo's three profiles, and Chapter 10 reviews and closes with the module's law: every counter power is a profile decision with a named owner.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Before the profile: ten records that must exist
lessons.html:
The profile points at records that must already exist in the back office. If they are right, creating the profile takes minutes. If they are wrong — the wrong company, a wrong warehouse — sales post incorrectly and correcting the postings afterwards can take days. Check this list, in this order, before creating any profile.

1. Company. The legal entity that will own the sales. Confirm its default currency and chart of accounts. A profile pointed at the wrong company posts every sale into the wrong set of books.

2. Cost centre. Where the shop's trading is recorded for reporting. The usual pattern is one cost centre per branch, which is what makes per-branch profit figures possible later.

3. Warehouse. The stock location the till sells from. This must be a leaf warehouse — an actual location, not a group heading. The till can only sell what this warehouse holds, and the profile will not accept a group.

4. Branch. The record that represents the shop itself. It ties the company, warehouse and cost centre together, and it is the record each terminal gets locked to during commissioning (module 3). Name branches clearly and distinctly — during commissioning someone will pick the branch from a list, and picking the wrong one sends sales to the wrong shop.

5. Price list. A selling price list in the company currency, with rates loaded for the items the counter will sell. Chapter 3 covers the rules about rates and their validity dates.

6. Sales tax template. The profile will not save without one. Tax on every bill is calculated from this template.

7. Payment methods. One record for each way money can arrive — cash, card, transfer, and so on. Chapter 3 covers the three method names with special behaviour.

8. Customer group and territory defaults. Where customers created at the counter are filed. Deciding these up front means every cashier files new customers the same way.

9. A walk-in customer. The single customer record that unnamed sales book to. Create one deliberately; do not let each cashier invent their own.

10. User accounts. One account per cashier, each with a working email address and a password the person knows. The email matters: the one-time approval codes from module 1 are delivered to approver emails, and password resets need them too.

The final check: sell one item from the back office. Before commissioning any terminal, complete one sale end to end from the back office itself, using the same warehouse and tax template the profile will use. If that sale posts cleanly, the foundation is sound — the till is a fast front end onto the same posting machinery, so a clean back-office sale means the item, price, tax, warehouse and accounts are all correctly wired. If it fails, you have found the problem before a terminal added its own variables. Do this once per branch and keep the test invoice number in your setup notes.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Items, prices, tax and payment methods
lessons.html:
Every scan at the till touches an item record, a price, a tax template and eventually a payment method. This chapter covers the rules for each — including three that cause most of the pricing problems seen in practice.

Items. The fields that matter at the counter:

• Barcode, if the shop scans, and a reasonably short item name — long names are cut off in the cart display.
• Taxable flag. Tick it for standard-rated goods, leave it off for exempt ones. The till honours it per line, so a mixed basket taxes correctly.
• Batch and serial settings. An item that should be tracked by batch or serial must be created that way on the item record. If it is not, the till has no way to ask which batch or serial is being sold.
• Non-stock items are supported for services and fees — they skip stock checks.
• Kiosk flags mark which items appear when a terminal runs in kiosk mode.

Prices — and the zero-rate trap. Rates are loaded against the profile's selling price list. Two rules to memorise: 1) An item with no valid rate scans at zero. The till flags it but does not block the sale — so an unpriced item can be sold for nothing while everyone assumes it had a price. 2) A rate outside its validity window counts as no rate at all. A rate whose start date has not arrived, or whose end date has passed, is ignored — this is the usual cause when items suddenly ring up at nil. When you get a pricing complaint, check the rate's validity dates first. Also note: where a batch carries its own price, the batch price is used ahead of the list rate. Price changes reach terminals on the next price refresh — no restart is needed.

Tax — one template per treatment. Tax is calculated from the profile's tax template at the moment the bill is created. Two settings interact: the per-item Taxable flag, and the profile's Is Tax Inclusive switch (whether shelf prices already contain tax). Here is the trap: switching Is Tax Inclusive rewrites the tax template itself, marking its lines as included in the printed price or not. So if two profiles with opposite tax treatments point at the same template, each save rewrites the other's behaviour, and both counters tax wrongly in turn. The rule: give each tax treatment its own template. An inclusive-priced counter and an exclusive-priced counter must never share one.

Payment methods. Every tender is a payment method record added to the profile's payments table. The order of rows in that table is the order cashiers see on the payment screen — put the most-used method first. Three method names have special behaviour built in:

• Cash prompts for the amount tendered, calculates change, opens the drawer, and works offline.
• Store Credit draws down the customer's stored balance. The balance lives on the server, so store credit is unavailable offline — a balance the till cannot verify is a balance it will not spend.
• Gift Voucher appears automatically when vouchers are enabled on the profile.

Card, transfer and similar methods simply record the amount — no live call is made, so they work offline. The exception is an integrated card terminal, covered on the Integrations tab in Chapter 8.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Tab 1: Setup
lessons.html:
The Setup tab holds the counter's day-to-day operating settings: customer defaults, cart behaviour, stock behaviour, shift management, and terminal switches. Field by field:

Customer defaults.

• Default customer group / territory — where counter-created customers are filed (decided in Chapter 2).
• Allow Duplicate Customer Names — when off, the till refuses to create a second customer with a name that already exists. Leave it off unless genuinely common names cause repeated blocks; if you turn it on, rely on the monthly duplicate scan (module 6) to merge the results.
• Max Items in Search Results — caps the product grid so search stays fast on modest hardware.

Cart rules.

• Allow Clear Cart — whether a cashier can discard a basket. Note the interplay with approvers: when this is off but a Power Approver holds the Clear Cart permission, the Clear button still appears but requires an approval. That makes discarding a basket a recorded, authorised event rather than an impossible one — which matters, because building a basket, taking cash, and then clearing instead of completing is a known fraud pattern (module 8 covers how to check for it).
• Clear Cart On Logout — whether an unfinished basket survives a sign-out. Turn it on where an abandoned basket must never carry over to the next cashier.
• Allow Checkout Item Update — whether quantities can still be edited on the payment screen.
• Enable Item Queue Options — adds a toggle at the till between stack mode (re-scanning an item increases its existing line) and queue mode (each scan makes its own line — useful where each unit needs its own serial or batch).
• Delete Cart Queue / Delete After (days) — automatic housekeeping for held baskets: parked carts older than the set age are removed.

Inventory and stock.

• Allow Viewing Other Warehouses — lets the counter answer is-it-at-the-other-branch questions from the Inventory Ops screen.
• Allow Negative Stock — permits selling below recorded stock. This setting mirrors a company-wide stock setting and will not save unless that setting also allows it. The profile cannot quietly permit what the company's inventory policy forbids, so treat a request to enable it as an inventory-policy question, not a till setting.
• Enable Auto Allocate Batch — the till picks batches automatically, oldest first, and only asks the cashier when the quantity cannot be covered. Turn it on for goods with expiry dates (oldest-first keeps stock rotating); leave it off where the cashier should choose, for example serialised or mixed-provenance goods.

Shift, terminal and access.

• Enable Shift Management — requires a shift to be opened before selling and closed with a counted drawer. Any counter that handles cash should have this on; module 4 covers the routine.
• Enable Offline Login — lets a cashier sign in against the terminal's stored record when the server is unreachable. It requires a prior successful online sign-in on that terminal, and expires seven days after the last one. Turn it on wherever power or connectivity is unreliable.
• Enable Kiosk Mode — the self-service display of kiosk-flagged items.
• Enable Messages — the Message Hub on this counter. Turn it off at counters that should not handle transfer requests.
• Allow Transaction Date Edit — permits back-dating a sale (never future-dating). Grant this sparingly: a back-dated sale moves revenue from one reporting day to another.
• Enable Airtime Sales — the Airtime console (module 6), switched per counter.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Tab 2: Pricing & Discounts
lessons.html:
The Pricing & Discounts tab decides how a cashier can reduce a price. Its first field is the most consequential setting on the whole profile.

Discount Mode. Three options, each a different way of controlling discounts:

• Standard. The cashier types a discount directly on the line. If the profile requires an override, an approver clears it at that moment. This suits a small shop with a supervisor on the floor — it is fast, and exactly as controlled as the supervisor's presence.
• Approval-based. Every discount must carry a reason chosen from the markdown reason list plus a typed explanation — neither can be blank. The reason is stored on the sale line and appears in markdown reporting, so at month end you can see not just how much was discounted but why. This is the recommended default for most businesses. Module 5 covers the markdown reasons themselves.
• Code-based. The cashier cannot type a discount at all. They raise a request from the cart; a category lead reviews it in the back office and approves (possibly changing the amount) or rejects; an approved request returns a single-use code the cashier applies. Every stage is timestamped. This gives the strongest control at the cost of a round trip, so it suits high-value negotiated goods rather than fast-moving counters. Module 5 walks the full cycle.

Choose the mode deliberately, based on the goods and the floor — do not leave it on its default.

Override Mode (password or one-time code). Where an approval is required, it can be given two ways, and the choice is a field here:

• Password — the approver enters their email and password at the till. Fast, and works offline, but the approver must be physically present.
• One-Time Code — the till requests a six-digit code, which is emailed to every approver holding the relevant permission; any of them can read it to the cashier by phone. Codes expire after one hour, and the terminal must be online to request one.

Pick password where a supervisor is resident; pick codes where approvers are often away. Note a useful side effect of the code design: because every code request is emailed to all holders of that permission, no discount can be quietly arranged with just one approver — the whole group sees every request.

The remaining fields.

• Allow Discount Edit — the master switch. Off, the discount control is disabled on every line regardless of mode. A counter that simply does not discount is one unticked box.
• Allow Rate Edit and Require Override for Rate Edit — rate editing lets a cashier overwrite the unit price itself, which is a stronger power than discounting (a discount is limited by the price; a rate edit replaces it). Edited lines are marked Rate override so they are visible on review. If you allow rate editing at all, turn the override requirement on as well.
• Enable Promotions / Enable Promotion Code — switches on the campaign machinery (module 5). One behaviour to know now: a line that has received a promotional discount is locked — no further manual discount or rate change can be added on top of it.
• Is Tax Inclusive — covered in Chapter 3; remember the shared-template rule.
• Allow Shipping Cost — adds an editable delivery fee line to the cart.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Tab 3: Payments & Returns
lessons.html:
The Payments & Returns tab governs credit, refunds, lay-by and staff purchases — every way money can leave later, leave backwards, or leave discounted.

Customer and payment settings.

• Allow Partial Payment — a sale can complete with less than full payment, the balance owing on the customer's account. This is the counter extending credit; only enable it where customer accounts are actually managed.
• Enable Credit Limit Check — shows the customer's balance and limit on the cart header, and suspends selling when the limit is breached (the cart shows: Sales suspended due to customer outstanding). Only a Power Approver holding the Credit Limit Override permission can release the sale. The release is a recorded approval.
• Allow Customer Credit Against Invoice — carries an unpaid balance on the invoice itself.
• Allow Loyalty Points — earning and redemption at this counter. Redemption is calculated on the server, so it is unavailable offline.

Returns. Four settings that work together:

• Allow Cash Refund — whether money can leave the drawer on a return. When off, the only refund route is store credit. Starting a new deployment with cash refund off is a sound default: store credit keeps the refund inside the system, while cash refunds open the drawer to the phantom-return pattern from module 1. Enable cash refunds later, deliberately, with the override requirement on.
• Allow Return Exchange — goods swapped for goods, with the difference settled in either direction.
• Require Override for Returns + Return Override Mode — every return needs an approver, by password or code as configured.
• Return Policy In Days (default thirty) — the return window. A return beyond the window is still possible, but requires an override — the window is a rule with a supervised exception, not a hard wall.

One visibility rule worth memorising: the Return & Exchange console only appears in the sidebar when at least one of cash refund, exchange, or the return policy is enabled. If none is enabled, there is no console at all — remember this when a returns menu seems to be missing.

Lay-By. Three numbers configure it:

• Lay-By Deposit % — the minimum taken when the lay-by is created (default ten).
• Lay-By Installments — how many payments the balance splits into (default three).
• Lay-By Day Spacing — comma-separated days from booking when instalments fall due; 0, 30, 90 means at once, after a month, after three months.

If the number of spacing values and the instalment count disagree, the count wins and the schedule is filled from the values available — but treat a mismatch as a mistake to fix, not behaviour to rely on. Provide exactly as many spacings as instalments.

Staff Purchase. Two fields here, plus dependencies elsewhere:

• Enable Staff Purchase — switches the console on for this counter.
• Staff Purchase Discount % — applied automatically to every line. If both this and a company-wide staff discount exist, the profile's percentage takes precedence at this counter.

For the feature to work end to end, three more things must exist: a purchase limit on each employee's record, and in the company-wide settings, the employee purchase account (where balances sit) and the salary component used to recover them through payroll. Module 6 covers the flow; set the wiring up here.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Tab 4: Gift Vouchers
lessons.html:
A gift voucher is a bearer instrument: whoever holds the code can spend it, exactly like cash. Because of that, everything on this tab is deliberately conservative — features are off until you turn them on, and each one you enable should be a considered decision. Module 7 covers running the voucher programme; this chapter covers its settings.

The core settings.

• Enable Gift Voucher — the master switch. It adds the voucher tile to the Sales Console and Gift Voucher as a payment method.
• Voucher Denominations — comma-separated face values shown as quick buttons when selling a voucher. Cashiers can still type another amount; the presets just speed up the common cases.
• Enable Voucher Partial Redemption — a voucher worth more than the bill keeps its remaining balance instead of being used up in one go.
• Voucher Change Policy — what happens to any surplus when a voucher exceeds the bill: Remainder as Balance keeps it on the voucher; No Change forfeits it. Decide this once, and make sure the printed terms match — customers will hold you to whichever was printed.

The offline policy — read this one carefully. A voucher's balance lives on the server, and a terminal that is offline cannot verify it. The Voucher Offline Policy field decides what happens then:

• Online Only (the default) — all voucher activity is refused while the terminal is offline, and the cashier is told so plainly. This is the safe choice: no voucher can be spent twice during an outage because none can be spent at all.
• Guarded Offline — voucher activity is permitted offline, within two limits you set: Offline Max Value (the largest single voucher redeemable offline) and Offline Daily Cap (the total voucher value one terminal may redeem offline per day). These caps are the business's maximum exposure if the same voucher is spent at two terminals during an outage. Set them by asking what the business can afford to lose on a bad day — and revisit them as voucher volumes grow.

The extended switches. Each off by default; enable only what the voucher programme actually needs:

• Enable Voucher Top-up — value can be added to an existing voucher.
• Enable Voucher Expiry — vouchers carry an expiry date and stop working after it. This is what makes lapsed-value accounting possible (module 7).
• Enable Corporate Vouchers — bulk voucher issues to a named corporate customer.
• Enable Refund to Voucher — a gift voucher can be a refund destination on returns, similar in spirit to store credit.
• Allow Voucher Buy-back — the shop redeems an unspent voucher for cash. This is the most dangerous switch on the tab, because it converts a bearer instrument directly into money out of the drawer. Leave it off unless there is a firm business reason, and if it must be on, require an override and watch its usage (module 8 explains what to watch).
• Enforce Voucher Booking — a voucher is reserved centrally before it can be issued at a counter. This closes the small window in which two tills could otherwise issue the same code at the same time. Any shop with more than one till should turn it on.

One rule to carry forward. Unless Guarded Offline was deliberately chosen, any sale that sells or redeems a voucher is refused while offline — and the till tells the cashier why. That refusal is the design working, not a fault.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Tab 5, the user table, and the Power Approvers
lessons.html:
The last tab, and the two tables that control who can do what.

Tab 5: Integrations. This tab wires an integrated card terminal to the till, so a card payment is pushed to the device and the till waits for the result (instead of the cashier keying the amount into a standalone machine).

• Enable Payment Gateway — the master switch.
• Live Environment — whether the connection points at the provider's live system or their test one. Follow this sequence exactly: commission with Live Environment off, process a successful test transaction, and only then switch it on. Note the switch date both times.
• Credentials — merchant identifier, public key, private key. The private key is stored masked. Treat these like passwords: store them properly, and rotate them if staff with access leave.
• Terminals table — one row per physical card machine, so the till knows which device receives a payment.

Offline behaviour: an integrated card payment needs a live connection. When offline, use cash, a manually keyed card entry, or transfer.

The user table. One row per person who signs in at this counter. Each row carries the person's account and a set of access boxes that decide which consoles they see:

• Standard — the Sales Console (ordinary selling).
• Order and Checkout — the two stages of Pharmacy mode. Note: the Checkout box also grants Revenue Intelligence access, since the person handling payment is the one who needs the money reports.
• Booking and Cashier — the two stages of Booking mode.
• Inventory Ops — stock enquiry, material requests and transfers. On by default.

Three mechanics to know: 1) The boxes are normalised against the profile's selling mode when the profile is saved — Standard mode grants everyone Standard and clears the two-stage boxes; Pharmacy clears the booking boxes. This is why module 1 said to set the mode first. 2) One row per user is marked as their default profile — the one they sign into automatically. 3) On sign-in, the till opens on the first console the person is entitled to: Sales in Standard mode, Checkout or Order in Pharmacy, Cashier or Booking in Booking mode; someone with only Inventory Ops lands there. Useful for support: where someone lands tells you what their row grants.

The Power Approver table. One row per approver, ticking only the permissions that person should hold: Discount, Returns (including beyond-window returns), Clear Cart, Rate, and Credit Limit Override. Grant each box deliberately — the boxes are independent, and module 1's Okelewo decision (Returns not bundled with Discount) is the pattern to copy.

The no-approver trap. If the profile requires an override for some action but no approver holds that permission, the control is simply disabled, and the cashier is told no approvers are configured. So: always configure at least one approver for every permission the profile requires — and before go-live, test every override path with a real approval. A discount that cannot be approved at six in the evening on opening day is a queue of customers and an emergency nobody needs.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: building Okelewo's profiles
lessons.html:
One afternoon of setup, using everything in this module. Okelewo builds three profiles — one per branch, since each branch's tills follow one policy.

The groundwork check (Chapters 2-3). The ten-record checklist runs first and finds three problems — which is normal, and is exactly why the checklist runs first:

• The Lagos shop had no leaf warehouse — a group warehouse had been standing in. A proper leaf warehouse is created before anything else.
• The price list contains about forty items whose rate validity windows have expired — each of these would have scanned at zero. The windows are fixed, and a quarterly price list review is added to the calendar so it does not recur.
• The draft plan pointed both the flagship (tax-inclusive shelf prices) and the Lagos shop (tax-exclusive) at one tax template. Chapter 3's rule applies: each treatment gets its own template, split before the first profile is saved.

The back-office test sale then posts cleanly at each branch. The payments table is ordered by actual frequency at the counter: cash, transfer, card. All eleven cashier accounts exist with working emails.

Tab 1 decisions (Chapter 4). Shift management on at all branches — the counted drawer is the point of the whole rollout. Offline login on — power in Abeokuta makes it necessary. Auto-allocate batch on at the flagship's provisions counter (expiry-dated goods, oldest first) and off at the Lagos electronics section (serials — the cashier should choose). Transaction date edit off for everyone. Duplicate customer names refused, with the monthly merge scan noted for module 6.

Tab 2 decisions (Chapter 5). Discount mode: Approval-based at all three branches — the MD wants to know why margin is given away, not just how much. Five markdown reasons are drafted (damaged, price match, display item, expiring stock, goodwill) for module 5. Override mode: password at the two Abeokuta shops, where supervisors are resident; one-time codes at Lagos, where the approver travels — accepting that code requests need the terminal online.

Tab 3 decisions (Chapter 6). Cash refund off at launch — refunds go to store credit only, to be revisited after ninety days of returns data. Returns override required, window thirty days. Lay-By: deposit raised to 15% after the MD weighs the risk of abandoned reservations, three instalments, spacing 0, 30, 60. Staff purchase enabled at the flagship only, with the employee purchase account and salary component confirmed in company settings before the switch is ticked.

Tab 4 (Chapter 7). Left dark for now, deliberately: the master switch stays off until the voucher accounts exist (the accountant's condition — module 7 opens with it). The launch design is agreed in advance: Online Only, booking enforcement on for the multi-till flagship, buy-back permanently off.

Tab 5, users and approvers (Chapter 8). No integrated card terminals yet, so the Integrations tab stays empty — noted as a decision, not an oversight. The user tables are filled after the mode is set (Standard everywhere for now). The approver table is built to module 1's casting: four approvers, boxes ticked per person, Returns not bundled with Discount, Credit Limit Override held by only two people. Then the go-live test from Chapter 8 catches a real one: the second Abeokuta shop's profile requires return overrides but has no approver row — on the test till, the return control shows disabled with the no-approvers message, exactly as the chapter warned. The row is added, and test every override path joins the permanent go-live checklist.

First sign-ins. Each cashier signs in; landing consoles and sidebars match what the rows grant. The MD's note at the end of the afternoon: we argued about checkboxes for four hours and I realised we were writing the shop's rules. Good. They were overdue.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Review & the second law
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section. Everything later in the track assumes this module.

Approach (Chapter 1). Every consequential field is decided on purpose, by the person who owns that policy, with the choice and reason noted. Profile changes on a live counter are rule changes — noted and reviewed. Profile count = policy count.

Groundwork (Chapter 2). Ten records before any profile: company, cost centre, leaf warehouse, branch (named unmistakably), price list, tax template, payment methods, customer group and territory defaults, one walk-in customer, and individual user accounts with working emails. Then one test sale from the back office — if it posts cleanly, the foundation is sound.

Items, prices, tax, tenders (Chapter 3). The taxable flag works per line; batch and serial tracking must be set when the item is created. An item with no valid rate scans at zero, and a rate outside its validity window is no rate at all — check validity dates first on any pricing complaint. Is Tax Inclusive rewrites the shared template, so each tax treatment gets its own template. The payments table's row order is the display order. Cash calculates change and works offline; Store Credit needs the server; Gift Voucher appears when vouchers are enabled.

Setup tab (Chapter 4). Clear Cart interacts with the approver table (off plus an approver = approval-required clearing). Stack versus queue mode. Held baskets age out. Negative stock mirrors the company setting. Auto-allocate picks oldest first. Shift management on for any cash counter. Offline login expires seven days after the last online sign-in. Transaction date edit moves revenue between reporting days — grant sparingly.

Pricing tab (Chapter 5). Discount Mode is the most consequential field: Standard (direct), Approval-based (reason plus explanation, stored on the line — the recommended default), Code-based (request, central approval, single-use code). Password approvals are fast and offline but need presence; one-time codes work remotely, email every holder, expire in an hour. Rate editing outranks discounting — mark it and require overrides. Promotional discounts lock their line.

Payments & Returns tab (Chapter 6). Credit limit breaches suspend the sale until a Credit Limit Override approver releases it. Cash refund off means store-credit-only — the sound launch default. Returns beyond the window need an override. The Return & Exchange console only appears when at least one returns feature is enabled. Lay-by: deposit %, instalments, day spacing — count wins on a mismatch. Staff purchase needs the employee limit, the purchase account and the salary component wired.

Voucher tab (Chapter 7). Everything off until deliberately on. Online Only is the safe offline policy; Guarded Offline is a chosen exposure with two caps. Booking enforcement for any multi-till shop. Buy-back converts vouchers to drawer cash — the most dangerous switch.

Integrations, users, approvers (Chapter 8). Live Environment: test first, then switch. Access boxes normalise to the mode on save; Checkout carries Revenue Intelligence; the landing console reveals the row. Approver permissions are five independent boxes. No approver for a required permission = a disabled control — configure at least one, and test every override path before go-live.

The second law: every counter power is a profile decision with a named owner. Module 3 takes the finished profiles to the hardware: installing, licensing and commissioning the terminals.

questions.q: A profile field left on its default is:
opts: Still a policy — just one nobody chose; consequential fields should be decided on purpose
questions.why: Decisions, noted with who and why.

questions.q: Who should decide the discount mode?
opts: Whoever owns pricing and margin — the administrator enters the decision
questions.why: The right people decide; the admin holds the pen.

questions.q: Editing a live profile:
opts: Changes the counter's rules for every sale after it — note the change and its reason
questions.why: Easy to make, easy to forget — hence the notes and the yearly review.

questions.q: The till's warehouse must be:
opts: A leaf warehouse — an actual location, not a group heading
questions.why: The profile will not accept a group.

questions.q: Branches should be named clearly because:
opts: A terminal is locked to a branch picked from a list during commissioning — a wrong pick sends sales to the wrong shop
questions.why: Chapter 2's naming rule pays off in module 3.

questions.q: Cashier accounts need working emails because:
opts: One-time approval codes and password resets are delivered to email
questions.why: The email is part of the control machinery.

questions.q: The pre-commissioning test is:
opts: One complete sale from the back office using the same warehouse and tax template — if it posts cleanly, the foundation is sound
questions.why: Find foundation problems before the terminal adds its own variables.

questions.q: An item with no valid rate on the price list:
opts: Cannot be added to the cart
Scans at zero — flagged but not blocked
questions.why: The classic silent leak.

questions.q: Two profiles with opposite tax treatments must not share a template because:
opts: Switching Is Tax Inclusive rewrites the template itself — each save would undo the other's behaviour
questions.why: One template per tax treatment.

questions.q: The order of rows in the payments table:
opts: Is the order cashiers see on the payment screen — put the most-used method first
questions.why: Display order is a choice.

questions.q: Store Credit is unavailable offline because:
opts: The customer's balance lives on the server and cannot be verified from the terminal
questions.why: A balance the till cannot check is a balance it will not spend.

questions.q: Allow Clear Cart off, plus an approver holding Clear Cart, means:
opts: The Clear button appears but requires an approval — discarding a basket becomes a recorded event
questions.why: Relevant to the take-cash-then-clear fraud pattern.

questions.q: Auto Allocate Batch picks:
opts: Batches automatically, oldest first, asking only when the quantity cannot be covered
questions.why: Good for expiry-dated goods; off where the cashier should choose.

questions.q: Allow Negative Stock:
opts: Mirrors a company-wide stock setting and will not save unless that setting also allows it
questions.why: The profile cannot override company inventory policy.

questions.q: Offline login expires:
opts: Seven days after the cashier's last successful online sign-in on that terminal
questions.why: Why cashiers should sign in online at least weekly.

questions.q: Allow Transaction Date Edit is granted sparingly because:
opts: A back-dated sale moves revenue from one reporting day to another; future dates are never allowed
questions.why: Reporting integrity behind one checkbox.

questions.q: The most consequential setting on the profile is:
opts: Discount Mode — it decides how a cashier can reduce a price
questions.why: Choose it deliberately, never by default.

questions.q: Approval-based mode requires every discount to carry:
opts: A reason from the markdown list plus a typed explanation — neither can be blank
questions.why: Month-end reporting can then say why margin was given.

questions.q: In Code-based mode, the cashier:
opts: Cannot type a discount at all — they request one, and apply the single-use code a category lead approves
questions.why: The strongest control, at the cost of a round trip.

questions.q: One-time approval codes:
opts: Are emailed to every approver holding the relevant permission, and expire after one hour
questions.why: The whole group sees every request — no quiet arrangements.

questions.q: Rate editing is stronger than discounting because:
opts: A discount is limited by the price; a rate edit replaces the price itself — so mark it and require an override
questions.why: Edited lines carry the Rate override marker.

questions.q: A line with a promotional discount:
opts: Is locked — no manual discount or rate change can be added on top
questions.why: Campaign discounts do not stack with manual ones.

questions.q: A customer over their credit limit:
opts: Suspends the sale until an approver with Credit Limit Override releases it — a recorded approval
questions.why: The cart shows: Sales suspended due to customer outstanding.

questions.q: With Allow Cash Refund off:
opts: The only refund route is store credit — a sound default for new deployments
questions.why: Cash refunds are enabled later, deliberately, with overrides.

questions.q: A return beyond the policy window:
opts: Is still possible but requires an override — a rule with a supervised exception
questions.why: Thirty days by default.

questions.q: The Return & Exchange console appears only when:
opts: At least one of cash refund, exchange, or the return policy is enabled
questions.why: Remember this when a returns menu seems missing.

questions.q: If lay-by spacing values and the instalment count disagree:
opts: The count wins and the schedule fills from the values available — fix the mismatch anyway
questions.why: Provide as many spacings as instalments.

questions.q: For staff purchase to work end to end, you need:
opts: The profile switch and discount, plus each employee's purchase limit, the employee purchase account, and the payroll salary component
questions.why: The profile's percentage takes precedence over the company-wide one.

questions.q: The voucher tab is conservative because:
opts: A voucher is a bearer instrument — whoever holds the code can spend it, like cash
questions.why: Everything off until deliberately on.

questions.q: Guarded Offline's two caps represent:
opts: The business's maximum exposure if a voucher is double-spent during an outage — the largest single voucher and the daily total per terminal
questions.why: Set by what the business can afford to lose on a bad day.

questions.q: Enforce Voucher Booking:
opts: Reserves a voucher centrally before issue, closing the window where two tills could issue the same code
questions.why: Any shop with more than one till should enable it.

questions.q: The most dangerous voucher switch is:
opts: Buy-back — it converts a bearer instrument directly into cash out of the drawer
questions.why: Off unless there is a firm reason; override and watch it if on.

questions.q: The Live Environment sequence is:
opts: Commission with it off, process a successful test transaction, then switch it on — noting the date both times
questions.why: Test first, then live.

questions.q: If a required override permission has no approver configured:
opts: The control is disabled and the cashier is told no approvers are configured — so configure at least one and test every path before go-live
questions.why: Okelewo hit exactly this on the test till.

questions.q: Module 2's law is:
opts: Every counter power is a profile decision with a named owner
questions.why: Decided on purpose, noted, and reviewed.

terminal_estate.title: POS 3 — Commissioning & the Terminal Estate
terminal_estate.desc: Installing and managing terminals: the installer and sync service, the four-step wizard with the branch lock, activation and licensing with the mode precedence rule, printer/drawer/display configuration tested with real sales, terminal settings and label templates, cached cashiers and the leaver procedure, and the device register with revocation and the monthly last-seen review.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Terminals as managed equipment
lessons.html:
This module covers everything between a bare computer and a working, licensed till: installation, the setup wizard, licensing, hardware, terminal settings, cached cashiers, and the device register. The module's law: a terminal is commissioned once and managed for its whole life.

Treat terminals as managed equipment. Every terminal in the business should have: a clear name, a branch it is locked to, a licence slot it occupies, a record in the device list, and a note of when and by whom it was set up. ZhiftPOS provides the tools for all of this — the setup wizard, the licence system, and the registered devices list — and this module shows how to use each one.

Why it matters. Two problems occur wherever terminals are set up casually:

• The badly commissioned terminal. Set up in a hurry by whoever was free: named DESKTOP-7XK2P, locked to the wrong branch (or the right one by luck), hardware half-tested. It works until the first return, the first offline period, or the first question about which shop a sale belongs to.
• The forgotten terminal. Set up correctly and then never managed again: retired machines still holding licence slots, a lost laptop still able to post sales, a device list nobody reads. Module 8's fraud chapter notes what a forgotten, still-enrolled terminal is worth to the wrong person.

Both problems have the same fix: a fixed commissioning procedure at the start, and the device register for everything after.

Time expectations. The first terminal at a site takes about forty minutes, including hardware. Each one after that takes about ten, because the decisions are already made and the procedure is already written. If your fifth terminal still takes forty minutes, the procedure is not written down.

The commissioning sequence. The chapters follow the order you work in:

1. Install the application and connect the hardware (Chapter 2).
2. Run the setup wizard: server, connection, branch lock, updates (Chapter 2).
3. Activate against the branch licence (Chapter 3).
4. Configure and test the printer, cash drawer and customer display (Chapter 4).
5. Set the terminal's own settings and label templates (Chapter 5).
6. Cache the cashiers who will use it (Chapter 6).
7. Confirm its entry in the device register (Chapter 7).

Chapter 8 shows Okelewo commissioning five terminals across three branches, and Chapter 9 reviews. Keep a short file per terminal as you go — the wizard choices, the licence slot, the hardware test results. That file is the terminal's service record, and Chapter 7 explains where it pays off.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Installation and the setup wizard
lessons.html:
Installing.

1. Run the installer with rights to install software. The installer also installs the background sync service and sets it to start automatically with the terminal.
2. Connect the hardware now — receipt printer, cash drawer, customer display — and confirm the operating system can see each device before configuring anything in ZhiftPOS. The application can only use devices the operating system already recognises; configuring first and plugging in later is the cause of half of all hardware problems.
3. Name the machine at the operating-system level to match the counter — the same name the profile uses, for example LALUBU-TILL-1. This name appears in the device list and in every support conversation for years. Set it now, while it costs nothing.
4. Launch the application. It opens on an unconfigured sign-in screen.

The setup wizard. Open Server Settings from the gear icon. The wizard has four steps.

Step 1 — Server. Enter the back office's full address, including the protocol (https://...), then press Validate & Fetch. The application contacts the server, confirms it is reachable, and downloads the connection details and branch list. If validation fails, check in this order: the address is typed correctly; the server is running; the terminal has a network route to it.

Step 2 — Connection. The web port, real-time path and real-time port are displayed for confirmation. They are filled in from the server and cannot be edited here. If they look wrong, the server's own configuration is wrong — fix it there. The wizard does not allow a terminal to override the server's connection facts.

Step 3 — Branch. Choose the terminal's branch from the fetched list and confirm. This choice locks the device to that branch. Notes:

• If the list is empty, press Reload. If it stays empty, either the branches have no warehouse assigned, or the server address points at the wrong system.
• Read the branch name carefully before confirming. A terminal locked to the wrong branch posts every sale to the wrong shop, and the error is discovered in the postings.
• After the lock, reopening Server Settings requires administrator verification on the terminal. This is deliberate: it prevents a cashier from re-pointing a till at a different branch or server. Treat any unlock as an administrator action worth noting.

Step 4 — Updates. Choose whether the terminal downloads updates automatically. Recommended on for shops without technical staff on site. Changeable later in System Settings.

After the wizard. The terminal is bound to its server and branch, and is ready for activation (Chapter 3). Record in the terminal's file: the OS name, the branch chosen, the updates decision, and the date.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Activation and licensing
lessons.html:
How licensing works. Each branch is licensed for a number of devices. The first time a terminal signs in successfully, it registers itself against that branch's allowance and confirms its selling mode against the licence. There is no separate activation screen — the first sign-in is the activation.

Activation checklist.

1. Confirm a licence slot is free for the branch before commissioning day. The device list (Chapter 7) shows what is currently enrolled.
2. Perform the first sign-in yourself as the commissioning administrator, so the enrolment is recorded under a known account on a known date.
3. Confirm the till presents the expected consoles — this verifies the selling mode once, at the start (see the precedence rule below).
4. Note the activation in the terminal's file.

If activation is refused. A terminal is refused when the branch's allowance is already fully used. The fix is housekeeping, not a support call: open the device list, find a terminal that is no longer in use, and revoke it. Revoking frees its slot immediately. Retired, replaced and lost terminals should already have been revoked — an allowance full of forgotten machines is the usual cause of a refusal.

If the licence lapses. When the licence expires or cannot be validated, the terminal signs the user out gracefully. Two facts to know and to reassure the counter with:

• Nothing is wiped. The local data stays on the terminal.
• No queued sale is lost. The queue survives a lapse exactly as it survives a restart. The terminal simply stops accepting new work until the licence is restored.

A lapse is a commercial matter with a technical symptom: renew or revalidate the licence, and the terminal resumes where it stopped.

The precedence rule. Memorise this sentence: the selling mode on the licence takes precedence over the mode on the profile. A branch licensed for Standard shows the Standard consoles even if its profile is set to Pharmacy. Two consequences:

• When planning: if a counter needs the two-stage Pharmacy flow or Booking mode, confirm the branch's licence carries that mode before building the profile.
• When troubleshooting: if a till shows different consoles from what the profile says, check the licence. Module 1's rule was: a missing menu item means check the profile. This chapter adds the second rule: wrong consoles overall means check the licence.

Summary. Know the branch's allowance before you start; activate under a known account; verify the mode once; revoke retired terminals to free slots; and remember that a lapse pauses the terminal without losing anything.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Receipt printer, cash drawer, customer display
lessons.html:
Hardware settings live in System Settings on the terminal, under the Printer and Display tabs. Configure each device, then test it the way described at the end of each section.

Receipt printer. Settings, in order:

• Enable printing — once the printer is installed at the operating-system level.
• Model family — Epson or Star. This selects the command language. Most thermal printers emulate Epson; check the printer's documentation.
• Installed printer — pick from the devices the operating system reports. Press Refresh after plugging a printer in; a stale list is the most common cause of nothing printing after the cable itself.
• Paper width — 80mm or 58mm. Set wrongly, receipts wrap or cut off their columns. This is the single most common printer misconfiguration.
• Copies — one, or two where a signed copy is kept.
• Print format — Standard Receipt (compact thermal layout) or Invoice Style (fuller page, for business customers).
• Font size — balance paper use against readability.
• Auto-print — on to print every receipt automatically; off where customers usually decline one.
• Header and footer — shop name, address, footer lines, and optionally the goods return policy text (it has its own switch and a length limit).

Test the printer with a real sale, not a test print. Procedure: sell one low-value item, print the receipt, then reverse the sale properly through Return & Exchange. A test page only proves the cable and driver. A real receipt exercises the totals, tax lines, header and footer — the parts that matter in a dispute. Keep the first real receipt in the terminal's file.

Cash drawer. Settings:

• Enable — only where a drawer is fitted. Enabled with no drawer produces harmless but confusing errors.
• Connection — Printer for the usual arrangement: the drawer is cabled to the receipt printer and opens on a pulse from it. (This is why a drawer that stops opening is often a printer-cable problem.) Custom Command for drawers that need their own instruction, entered as hexadecimal bytes from the drawer's documentation. None disables the trigger.
• Test Drawer — use it before go-live.

Operating fact: the drawer opens on completion of a cash sale. Module 4's shift routine depends on this, and module 8 notes that a drawer opening without a sale is something a supervisor should notice.

Customer (pole) display. Settings:

• Port — press Refresh after plugging in, then select.
• Baud rate — match the display's documentation; 9600 is the common default.
• Columns and rows — typically 20 by 2.
• Protocol — the command set. Known symptom: text appears but never clears between items → select the protocol variant that does not send a clear command.
• Line ending — change only if lines overwrite or wrap oddly.
• Port lock — keep the port held open unless another application needs it.
• Idle message — the scrolling text shown between customers.

Troubleshooting rule for garbled or overlapping text: change one setting at a time, starting with the protocol. Changing several at once makes the working combination impossible to identify.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Label templates and terminal settings
lessons.html:
The profile/settings split. Keep this distinction clear, because it routes every configuration question: the POS Profile (module 2) holds the counter's policy — what may be done. System Settings on the terminal holds this machine's own behaviour — how this terminal operates. The discount mode is a profile question; the paper width is a terminal question.

System Settings has five tabs: Server & App, Printer, Display, Sync & Device, and Labels. Printer and Display were covered in Chapter 4; Sync & Device is Chapter 6. This chapter covers the other two.

Server & App tab.

• Connection details — the server, ports and branch from the wizard, shown read-only, with the validation status.
• Inventory cache limit — how many product rows the terminal stores locally. Rule: set it at or above the catalogue size. A limit below the catalogue means some items are simply not present in the local copy — and those items cannot be found while offline. When an item cannot be found offline, check sync first, then this limit. Raise it for large catalogues; lower it only on genuinely constrained hardware.
• Full screen mode — hides the title bar. Usual choice for a dedicated till.
• Fast checkout — completes sales instantly and posts them in the background. Leave it off at commissioning. Module 8 explains the trade-off and when to enable it; until then, the default is off.
• Updates — the wizard's step-4 choice, adjustable here. Keep the update posture consistent across the estate.

Labels tab. Label templates control shelf-edge and product labels, printed from the Label Printing console (module 6). A template defines:

• Layout — name, price and barcode, or name and barcode only.
• Label size — width, height, and barcode height, in millimetres.
• Type sizes — point sizes for the name and the price.
• Item code — shown or hidden.
• Sheet geometry (for sheet printers) — paper size, the four margins, column and row gaps, and column count. A column count of zero means fit as many as the paper allows.

Working practice:

1. Start from a supplied preset rather than a blank template.
2. Adjust, then use Save as new — the preset stays intact and your variant gets its own name.
3. Print one sheet on plain paper and hold it against a real label sheet before committing label stock. One plain page costs nothing; a misaligned roll of labels is money in the bin.

Estate consistency. Keep the terminal posture deliberate and uniform: the same cache rule, the same update stance, the same proven templates across the terminals of a branch. A uniform estate is why the tenth terminal takes ten minutes — and why any terminal can be diagnosed by comparing it with its neighbours.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Cached cashiers
lessons.html:
The Sync & Device tab lists the cashiers this terminal remembers — the people who can sign in when the server is unreachable. Where the profile enables offline login (module 2), a cashier who has signed in online on this terminal is cached and can afterwards sign in offline.

The three states. Each cached cashier shows one of:

• Ready — can sign in offline right now.
• Re-login required — the stored credentials were rejected. The cashier must sign in once while online to refresh them. Until they do, their queued sales cannot post. This makes a Re-login state urgent, not cosmetic: the person's completed sales are waiting on it.
• Locked — more than seven days have passed since their last successful online sign-in on this terminal. Offline access has expired; an online sign-in restores it.

The weekly rule. Because of the seven-day expiry: every cashier should sign in online at least once a week on each terminal they use offline. Put this on the branch's weekly routine (module 8's calendar) rather than trusting memory — the cashier who only ever works through outages is exactly the one who gets locked out during one.

When a cashier leaves. Use Forget cashier on this tab, and treat leaving as a three-record procedure, all on the same day:

1. Remove the person's row from every POS Profile that lists them (module 2's user table).
2. Forget their cached entry on every terminal they used. List the terminals from the device register rather than from memory.
3. Disable their back-office user account.

Why all three: a departed cashier whose cached entry survives on a back-room terminal can still sign in offline there, and sales made that way are attributed to them. Closing all three records the same day removes the possibility.

Manager override sign-in. When an offline sign-in is refused because the terminal has no cached record of the cashier, a manager can sign the cashier in using the manager's own credentials. Two built-in properties:

• The sales made in that session are tagged for audit.
• The cashier is told about the tagging at the time.

Use the override as what it is — a way to keep a counter trading through a gap — and not as a routine substitute for proper caching. Because every override session is tagged, a monthly count of them is easy: the healthy number is near zero, and each one should have a known story. A branch that quietly runs on manager overrides because onboarding never cached anyone will show up immediately in that count.

Commissioning step. When commissioning a terminal, have each cashier who will use it sign in online once, then confirm the list shows them all as Ready. That is the terminal's people, set deliberately.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The device register
lessons.html:
The registered devices list in the back office is the record of every terminal in the business. One row per terminal, carrying:

• Identifier and label — the label is the OS-level name from Chapter 2, which is why that name was worth setting properly.
• Branch and profile — what the terminal is bound to.
• Enrolled by / enrolled on — who performed the activation sign-in, and when.
• Last seen — when the terminal last communicated with the back office.
• Status — active or revoked.

Revoking. Revoke a device when it is retired, replaced, lost, stolen or sold. Record who revoked it and why on the revocation. Effects:

• A revoked device can no longer post sales.
• Its history remains — the record is closed, not deleted.
• Its licence slot is freed immediately (Chapter 3's remedy for a full allowance).

The rule: no terminal leaves service without a revocation. A lost machine that was never revoked is still enrolled and still able to post into the business's records from wherever it is — the hardware version of a departed employee whose account was never disabled.

The last-seen review. Once a month, scan the last-seen column for terminals that have not communicated recently. Three possible meanings, in rising order of concern:

1. A closed counter — seasonal or temporary. Fine; note it.
2. A dead or retired terminal — revoke it and update the register.
3. A terminal that is trading but not syncing — the serious one. Its queue is growing unposted and its prices are going stale. Investigate the same day: usually the sync service has stopped, or the network path has broken.

The monthly scan takes two minutes. Without it, case 3 is typically discovered weeks later, with a large queue to untangle and stale figures in between.

The terminal's file. Everything this module produces per terminal belongs in one place — the file started in Chapter 1: wizard choices, licence slot, hardware test results (including the first real receipt), settings decisions, cached-cashier list, and later, any revocation. The register plus these files is the estate's memory: any terminal's history answerable without relying on whoever set it up.

Recurring tasks from this module (collected into module 8's calendar):

• Monthly — last-seen review; licence allowance check.
• On staff change — the three-record procedure from Chapter 6.
• On terminal change — revoke with who-and-why; commission the replacement by the standard procedure.
• Yearly — walk the register: every row's branch, profile and label still correct; files complete.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: Okelewo commissions five terminals
lessons.html:
Okelewo commissions five terminals across three branches. The events below are the ones worth learning from.

The first terminal (flagship). The old standalone till is replaced first, following the Chapter 2 procedure exactly: hardware connected and visible to the operating system before configuration, the machine named LALUBU-TILL-1 to match the counter, and the wizard run step by step. At step 3, the branch list shows two confusingly similar names — the flagship and a draft record for the second Abeokuta shop. Rather than guessing, the administrator pauses and renames the draft branch in the back office so the two cannot be mistaken, then completes the lock. Total time: forty-one minutes, as expected for a first terminal. A one-page commissioning checklist is written from the session; every later terminal follows it.

The licence refusal (Lagos). The Lagos terminal's activation is refused: the branch's allowance is already fully used. The device list explains it in one look — a trial-era terminal, dead in a storeroom for a year, is still enrolled and holding the slot. It is revoked (reason recorded: retired hardware, never deprovisioned), the slot frees immediately, and the new terminal activates within the hour. Follow-up: a full census of the register against physical reality runs that week and finds one more ghost — a repaired machine that had been enrolled twice. Both corrected; the monthly last-seen review goes on the calendar with the operations lead's name on it.

The hardware tests. The flagship printer configures as Epson, 80mm, and the real-sale test prints cleanly. At the second Abeokuta shop, the settings had been copy-pasted from the flagship — and the real-sale test immediately shows wrapped, broken columns: the physical printer there is a 58mm machine. One setting change, one more test sale, fixed — caught on a test receipt instead of on a customer's. The Lagos cash drawer does not respond to the printer pulse; its documentation supplies a custom hexadecimal command, which is entered and confirmed with Test Drawer. The flagship's pole display shows garbled text on first connection; following the one-setting-at-a-time rule, the protocol is changed first — fixed on the first change. Label templates are adjusted from a preset, saved as new, and proven on plain paper before any label stock is used.

The people and the valve. At each terminal, the branch's cashiers each sign in online once; the Sync & Device list is confirmed all-Ready. At the flagship, the manager override is deliberately tested once: a cashier who had never used that terminal is refused offline, the supervisor signs her in on his credentials, and the audit tag is then verified visible in the back office — with the counter staff watching. The point of doing it publicly: everyone now knows the override works, and everyone knows it is recorded.

Result. The fifth terminal takes eleven minutes and produces the same one-page file as the first. The MD's note: I have bought machines for nine years; this is the first time I have owned an estate.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Review & the third law
lessons.html:
Check yourself against each section before the quiz.

Installation (Chapter 2). The installer also installs the background sync service, set to start with the terminal. Hardware is connected and OS-visible before it is configured in ZhiftPOS. The machine is named at the OS level to match the counter.

The wizard (Chapter 2). Step 1: server address with protocol, Validate & Fetch; failures mean wrong address, server down, or no route — in that order. Step 2: connection details are read-only; if wrong, fix the server. Step 3: the branch choice locks the device; an empty list means branches without warehouses or the wrong server; reopening Server Settings afterwards requires administrator verification. Step 4: auto-updates, recommended on where no technical staff are on site.

Licensing (Chapter 3). Each branch has a device allowance; the first sign-in registers the terminal against it. A refusal means the allowance is full — revoke an unused device to free a slot. A lapse signs out gracefully: nothing is wiped, no queued sale is lost. And the precedence rule: the licence's selling mode overrides the profile's — wrong consoles overall means check the licence.

Hardware (Chapter 4). Printer: model family, refreshed device list, and above all the correct paper width (80mm vs 58mm). Test with a real sale, not a test print — the real receipt proves totals, tax and footer. Drawer: usually opens on a pulse from the printer (so check the printer cable when it stops); custom hex command otherwise; opens on completion of a cash sale. Display: baud, columns, protocol; text that never clears means pick the no-clear-command protocol variant; and always change one setting at a time.

Terminal settings and labels (Chapter 5). Profile = policy; System Settings = this machine. Inventory cache limit at or above the catalogue size, or items go missing offline. Fast checkout stays off until module 8's judgment. Labels: start from a preset, Save as new, and prove one sheet on plain paper before using label stock.

Cached cashiers (Chapter 6). Ready / Re-login required (their queued sales cannot post until they sign in online) / Locked (seven days). Weekly online sign-in rule. Leaving = three records, same day: profile rows, cached entries on every terminal (listed from the register), back-office account. Manager override sign-ins are tagged for audit and the cashier is told; monthly count near zero.

The register (Chapter 7). One row per terminal: label, branch, profile, enrolled by/on, last seen, status. Revoke retired/lost/replaced devices with who-and-why — revocation blocks posting, keeps history, frees the slot. Monthly last-seen review; the dangerous case is the terminal trading without syncing. One file per terminal.

The third law: a terminal is commissioned once and managed for its whole life — named, locked, licensed, tested with real sales, its people cached and removed on time, and its record kept from enrolment to revocation. Module 4 moves to the trading day itself.

questions.q: The two classic terminal-management failures are:
opts: The badly commissioned terminal and the forgotten terminal — fixed by a standard procedure and the device register
questions.why: Ceremony at the start; register for life.

questions.q: The first terminal takes about forty minutes; later ones take about ten because:
opts: The decisions are already made and the procedure is written down
questions.why: If the fifth still takes forty, the procedure is not written.

questions.q: Hardware should be connected:
opts: Before configuration, and confirmed visible to the operating system first
questions.why: The app can only use devices the OS already sees.

questions.q: The machine's OS-level name should:
opts: Match the counter — it appears in the device list and support conversations for years
questions.why: Set it while it costs nothing.

questions.q: Step 2's connection details cannot be edited because:
opts: They come from the server — if they look wrong, the server's configuration is what needs fixing
questions.why: A terminal cannot override the server's connection facts.

questions.q: Choosing the branch at step 3:
opts: Locks the device to that branch; reopening Server Settings then needs administrator verification
questions.why: It prevents a cashier re-pointing a till.

questions.q: An empty branch list that stays empty after Reload means:
opts: The branches have no warehouse assigned, or the address points at the wrong system
questions.why: Two causes to check.

questions.q: Activation happens:
opts: At the first successful sign-in — the terminal registers against the branch's device allowance
questions.why: Do it under a known admin account and note the date.

questions.q: Activation refused for a full allowance is fixed by:
opts: Revoking an unused terminal in the device list — the slot frees immediately
questions.why: Usually a forgotten machine is holding the slot.

questions.q: When a licence lapses:
opts: The terminal signs out gracefully — nothing is wiped and no queued sale is lost
questions.why: Renew the licence; the terminal resumes where it stopped.

questions.q: If the licence says Standard and the profile says Pharmacy:
opts: Standard shows — the licence's selling mode takes precedence over the profile's
questions.why: Wrong consoles overall = check the licence.

questions.q: Before building a two-stage Pharmacy profile you should:
opts: Confirm the branch's licence carries that mode
questions.why: The precedence rule applies at planning time too.

questions.q: The most common printer misconfiguration is:
opts: Wrong paper width — 80mm vs 58mm; receipts wrap or cut off columns
questions.why: One field, checked against the physical machine.

questions.q: Printers are tested with:
opts: A real sale — sold, printed, then properly reversed; it proves totals, tax and footer
questions.why: A test page only proves the cable and driver.
